title: The Family Media Agreement
tagline: A student leads their whole household in building a family media plan the way doctors recommend, covering sleep, meals, content, and screen-free time, so the rules are made with everyone instead of handed to the kids.
groupSize: Prepared in class; built at home with the whole family; reviewed in class
overview: Most household screen rules are handed down and resented. Pediatric guidance suggests the opposite works better: a family media plan the whole household builds together, one that covers more than minutes, when devices sleep, whether screens come to meals, what content fits which ages, and protected screen-free time, and that holds adults to the same standards as kids. In this activity the student becomes the facilitator. They learn what a good media plan actually covers, practice running a fair family meeting in class, and then lead that meeting at home: gathering everyone's needs, proposing agreements, handling pushback, and writing a plan each person signs. The stance is balanced and realistic: the plan is not a ban list and not a promise that screens are harmless; it is a living agreement a family revisits, built on the idea that people follow rules they helped write. Students practice leadership, negotiation, and the self-advocacy of asking adults to model what they ask of kids.
objectives: Students will identify the parts of a strong family media plan beyond time limits (sleep, meals, content, screen-free time, modeling).
Students will facilitate a fair family meeting where every member's needs are heard.
Students will negotiate and record agreements the whole household will sign, including ones that apply to adults.
Students will build in a review date and explain why a living agreement beats a fixed rule.

print: Handout A: What a Good Plan Covers, a reference (1 per student)
Handout B: Run the Family Meeting, facilitator script and needs-gathering sheet (1 per student, taken home)
Handout C: Our Family Media Agreement (1 per student, completed and signed at home)
digital: Optional: the AAP online Family Media Plan tool, used by a family that prefers a digital version
Optional: a shared calendar to set the review-date reminder

prep: Print Handouts A, B, and C for every student.
Model the facilitator stance briefly: a good facilitator asks, listens, and summarizes rather than dictates.
Set the window for the home meeting and the class review day.
Add your name and the return date to the family note on Handout C.

steps.title: Rules you didn't help write
steps.body: Ask: **"Think of a screen rule you've been given that you ignore the second no one's watching. Why?"** Collect honest answers (didn't make sense, applied only to me, no one explained it). Then flip it: "What if you ran the meeting that made the rules? Today you learn to lead your family in building a media plan together, one that even applies to the grown-ups."
steps.note: Students light up at the idea of leading. Channel it toward fair facilitation, not toward writing rules that only benefit themselves.

steps.title: What a good plan covers
steps.body: Students read Handout A, which lays out what pediatric guidance says a family media plan should cover: device bedtimes (screens out of bedrooms overnight so sleep is protected), mealtimes, content and age-fit, protected screen-free activities, how everyone treats each other online, and, crucially, that adults follow the plan too. In pairs, students rank which parts their own family most needs. Debrief that a plan is much more than a number of minutes.
steps.note: The sleep piece is where evidence is strongest, so highlight device bedtimes. But keep the plan broad: minutes alone is the weakest, most-fought-over lever.

steps.title: Run a practice meeting
steps.body: In groups of four, students role-play a family meeting using Handout B's script. One facilitates; others play a tired parent, a younger sibling, and a teen. The facilitator practices the moves: open with purpose, gather each person's needs before proposing anything, propose an agreement, invite pushback, and find a version everyone can accept. Groups swap the facilitator role once so everyone practices leading and being heard.
steps.note: Coach the hardest move: gathering needs before proposing solutions. Students, like adults, want to jump to rules; the fair meeting starts with listening.

steps.title: Lead the real meeting at home
steps.body: At home, the student facilitates the actual family meeting with Handout B, then records agreements on Handout C across the plan's areas: device bedtimes and where phones charge, mealtime and screen-free times, content and age-fit for different family members, online kindness, and at least one agreement that applies to the adults. Everyone who agrees signs, and the family sets a review date. The student notes one place they had to compromise.
steps.note: Prepare students for real pushback and for households that differ (shift work, shared devices, multigenerational homes). A plan that fits the real family beats a textbook-perfect one.

steps.title: What held, what you'd change
steps.body: Back in class, students debrief in small groups: **"What was the hardest need to balance? What agreement surprised you? How did leading the meeting change how your family reacted compared with rules being imposed?"** Capture why shared, revisable agreements tend to stick. Close on the balanced idea: a media plan is a living agreement, not a verdict on whether screens are good or bad.
steps.note: Listen for students realizing that holding adults to the plan was both the hardest and the most powerful part. That mutual accountability is the heart of it.

unplugged: The whole activity runs on paper: the reference sheet, the role-play script, the needs sheet, and the signed agreement. The family meeting is a face-to-face conversation; no device is required to build or keep the plan.
digital: A family that prefers it can build the same plan with the AAP online Family Media Plan tool and keep a digital copy, and set the review date as a shared calendar reminder. The in-class role-play and reflection stay unplugged.
whyTech: This is paper-first because the learning is facilitation and negotiation among real people. The optional digital tool only stores the plan a family already built together; it adds convenience, not learning.

adaptations.label: Grade 6
adaptations.text: Provide a shorter plan with three areas (device bedtimes, mealtimes, screen-free time) and a simplified meeting script.
Students facilitate a plan that includes their own greater autonomy and responsibilities, and negotiate a transition toward self-managed limits rather than parent-set ones.

adaptations.label: Emergent bilinguals
adaptations.text: Offer the family note, script, and agreement in the home language and let the meeting happen in whatever language the family uses.

adaptations.label: Nontraditional households
adaptations.text: Adapt roles for the real household (one parent, grandparents, siblings, shared custody); the plan can even span two homes with slightly different agreements.

lookFors: Students name plan areas beyond minutes, especially device bedtimes for sleep, and can say why each matters.
In the role-play, the facilitator gathers everyone's needs before proposing agreements.
The signed agreement covers multiple areas and includes at least one agreement that applies to the adults.
The plan has a review date, and the student can explain why a revisable agreement outlasts an imposed rule.
reflection: Why do people follow rules they helped write more than rules handed to them? (Student ELE 4.1: I take responsibility for my own learning.)
What was it like to lead your family and still make sure everyone was heard? (Student ELE 3.1 and 3.2: teamwork and clear communication.)
Why does holding adults to the same plan matter, and how did your family respond to it?
transfer: Families keep the media agreement visible and revisit it on the review date. In class, the facilitation skills carry into student-led conferences or group work, where the same meeting structure, gather needs, propose, invite pushback, agree, helps teams make decisions together.

handouts.title: What a Good Plan Covers
handouts.instructions: A strong family media plan covers much more than minutes. With a partner, rank which of these your own family most needs to talk about.
items: Device bedtimes: screens out of bedrooms overnight so everyone's sleep is protected.
Charging spot: where all devices (including adults') rest and charge at night.
Mealtimes: whether and when meals are screen-free.
Screen-free activities: protected time for sleep, exercise, homework, and being together.
Content and age-fit: what shows, games, and apps fit which family members.
Online kindness and privacy: how we treat others online and what we keep private.
Adults too: which agreements apply to the grown-ups, not just the kids.
Flexibility: how the plan bends for trips, sick days, projects, and special events.
Review date: when we will revisit and adjust the plan together.

handouts.title: Run the Family Meeting
handouts.instructions: You are the facilitator. Use this script and gather everyone's needs BEFORE you propose any agreement. Family note: your student is practicing leading a fair meeting; please take part honestly and let them run it.

sections.prompt: OPEN: Say why we're meeting. ("We're building a family media plan together so the rules make sense and apply to everyone.") Write your opening line:
GATHER NEEDS: Go around. What does each person need or worry about with screens? (Write everyone's name and need, including the adults'.)
PROPOSE: Suggest agreements that try to meet those needs. Jot your first proposals:
INVITE PUSHBACK: Ask "What doesn't work about this?" and adjust. Note what you changed:

handouts.title: Our Family Media Agreement
handouts.instructions: Record what your family agreed to, then everyone signs. Remember: at least one agreement must apply to the adults, and set a date to revisit it.
